title: How did the planets get their names? | SPACE WORDS

entries.note: From Old English [[from:eorthe]], dirt, soil or country; like most languages' word for the world it comes from the ground, and may have been personified like [[see:Gaia]].
The more common old word for the material human world, recorded in [[see:Beowulf]] and heard today in the [[see:Marvel Universe]].
Latin for earth, sometimes used as another name for [[see:Earth]] to align it with the Latin-named planets; it was personified as a goddess.
Greek personification of the earth as a goddess, like [[see:Terra]]; also mother and wife of [[see:Uranus]].
An Old English word from about the sixth century, formed with [[from:-ling]], originally meaning a ploughman; now associated with an alien view of humans.
A Germanic diminutive suffix combining Old English [[from:-le]] and [[from:-ing]]; planets named after Roman gods take [[see:-ian]] instead.
The Latin-derived ending used for the other planets' inhabitants instead of [[see:-ling]].
An Old English ending that makes a tool or thing used for a purpose, as in [[see:thimble]] and [[see:handle]]; part of [[gave:-ling]].
An Old English ending forming verb tenses and participles; attached to [[see:-le]] it gave the diminutive [[gave:-ling]].
A thumb tool, an example of the [[see:-le]] ending.
A thing your hand can use, an example of the [[see:-le]] ending.
German for a refugee, someone who is fleeing, an example of the Germanic [[see:-ling]] suffix.
German for butterfly, an adorable example of the [[see:-ling]] suffix.
Someone who works for hire, an English example of [[see:-ling]].
A mocking term for a friar with a shaved head, formed with [[see:-ling]].
Old English for a young man with his first beard, formed with [[see:-ling]].
Greek for order, opposed to [[see:chaos]]; also an arrangement of decorations on fabric, suggesting a night sky decorated with stars.
The concept the Greek [[see:cosmos]], order, is directly opposed to.
Originally a bobbin, one of the space words from textile arts, like [[see:cosmos]].
Originally the tool that zips back and forth in a loom, hence a shuttle bus; a space word from textiles, like [[see:cosmos]].
A [[see:pleonasm]], since [[see:galaxy]] literally means milky, though the repetition goes unnoticed because that meaning is forgotten.
Redundant wording, more openly accepted and possibly more emphatic than a [[see:tautology]], as in [[see:Milky Way galaxy]].
Similar to a [[see:pleonasm]] but sometimes considered an error.
Literally milky, from Greek [[from:galaxias kyklos]], milky circle; related to [[same-root:lactose]].
Related to [[same-root:galaxy]], which literally means milky.
Literally wanderer, from Greek [[from:asteres planetai]], wandering stars, because planets seem to change direction in the sky as Earth overtakes them.
Has two pronunciations, one the butt of jokes; once called [[see:Georgium Sidus]], it is the only planet named after a Greek god, son and husband of [[see:Gaia]].
A NASA camp in Huntsville, Alabama, where children experience astronaut training and freeze-dried food; Jess went as a kid.
Name for [[see:Uranus]] after [[see:George III]]; once [[see:William Herschel]] identified it as a planet, it was called the Georgian Planet.
Identified [[see:Uranus]] as a planet in the late 1700s.
Corresponds to [[see:Poseidon]], name probably cognate with [[same-root?:nebula]]; identified in the 1800s from its pull on [[see:Uranus]], though [[see:Galileo]] had seen it.
Means cloudy; probably cognate with [[same-root?:Neptune]].
Had seen [[see:Neptune]] but taken it for a star.
Literally a thing high up in the air; once any atmospheric phenomenon, it narrowed to the fiery kind except in [[see:meteorology]].
Once the study of any atmospheric phenomenon, not just weather, keeping the broad old sense of [[see:meteor]].
Notable winds and tornadoes, one of the four old kinds of [[see:meteor]].
Water-based phenomena such as rain, snow, hail and dew, one of the four old kinds of [[see:meteor]].
Light-based phenomena such as auroras and rainbows, one of the four old kinds of [[see:meteor]].
Fiery-looking phenomena such as shooting stars, the sense [[see:meteor]] has narrowed to.
What a [[see:meteor]] becomes once it hits the ground.
Means long-haired, for the tail streaming behind it; comets are made of dust and ice.
Literally star-like or star-shaped, from [[from:aster]]; a rocky object orbiting the Sun, unlike a [[see:meteoroid]].
Unlike an [[see:asteroid]], it may just be flying around through space rather than orbiting the Sun.
Cube-shaped, a parallel to [[see:asteroid]], star-shaped.
Human-shaped, a parallel to [[see:asteroid]].
Something fact-shaped that is not a fact, a parallel to [[see:asteroid]].
The element meaning star in [[gave:asteroid]], [[gave:disaster]] and [[gave:astronaut]]; related to [[same-root:star]].
Related to [[same-root:aster]] and to the stellar element in [[same-root:constellation]].
Literally ill-starred, from [[from:aster]]: a terrible event foretold by the stars or caused by their bad alignment.
Literally a star sailor, from [[from:aster]]; it also came up with [[see:cosmonaut]] in the nautical terms episode.
Discussed with [[see:astronaut]] in the earlier episode about nautical terms.
Its poop comes from Latin [[from:Puppis]], also a constellation; Rob apologises again for having put the poop deck at the front of the ship.
A constellation named for the stern of the [[see:Argo]], and the Latin source of the poop in [[gave:poop deck]].
The ship in which [[see:Jason]] and his companions sought the Golden Fleece; [[see:Puppis]] is named for its stern.
Means shining together; its stellar element is related to [[same-root:star]].
A southern-hemisphere constellation with a Neo-Latin name, given much later than the Greek and Roman names of northern ones.
A scientific-sounding southern-hemisphere constellation name, alongside [[see:Telescopium]].
A scientific-sounding southern-hemisphere constellation name, alongside [[see:Microscopium]].
Named by the Greeks after the daughter of [[see:Cassiopeia]] and [[see:Cepheus]], sacrificed to a sea monster to appease [[see:Poseidon]] and rescued by [[see:Perseus]].
Mother of [[see:Andromeda]], whose boast that her daughter was sexier than the nymphs angered [[see:Poseidon]].
King and father of [[see:Andromeda]].
Married [[see:Andromeda]] after rescuing her from a sea monster.
The hunter, firing his arrow at [[see:Lepus]] while hunting with the dogs [[see:Canis Major]] and [[see:Canis Minor]].
One of [[see:Orion]]'s two hunting dogs; canis shares its root with the [[same-root:Canary Islands]] and [[same-root:canine]].
The other of [[see:Orion]]'s two hunting dogs, alongside [[see:Canis Major]].
Literally the dog islands, sharing a root with the canis of [[same-root:Canis Major]].
Shares a root with the canis of [[same-root:Canis Major]].
The hare constellation, at which [[see:Orion]] fires his arrow.
Commonly called the [[see:Big Dipper]], or in England the [[see:Plough]]; always visible in the northern polar sky, hence [[see:Arctic]].
Commonly called the [[see:Little Dipper]].
Common name for [[see:Ursa Major]].
Common name for [[see:Ursa Minor]].
The name most common in England for [[see:Ursa Major]].
From Greek [[from:arktos]], bear, because [[see:Ursa Major]] is always visible in the northern polar sky.
Literally opposite the bear, contrasting with [[see:Arctic]]; fittingly, polar bears live only in the north and penguins in the south.
From Greek [[from:zodiakos kyklos]], circle of little animals, though signs like [[see:Libra]] aren't animals; once called the [[see:twelve signs]], [[see:bestiary]] or [[see:Our Lady's way]].
A set of scales, one of the [[see:zodiac]] signs that isn't an animal.
Both the crab constellation and the disease, named because swollen vessels around cancerous cells resembled crab legs; from Greek [[from:karkinos]]; German uses one word for both.
Greek source of [[gave:cancer]], [[gave:carcinoma]] and [[gave:carcinogen]]; TikTok auto-captions once rendered Jess saying it as quirky nose.
Also from Greek [[from:karkinos]], like [[same-root:cancer]].
Also from Greek [[from:karkinos]], like [[same-root:cancer]].
The STD of genital lice, named for its appearance; in German, having crabs means having [[see:cancer]].
Old English name for the [[see:zodiac]].
A Middle English name sometimes used for the [[see:zodiac]].
A Middle English name for the [[see:zodiac]], referring to the path of the Moon.
In English from the 12th century for spiritual and scientific study alike; it became the scientific term in the 17th century, echoing Latin [[from:astronomia]].
In English from the 14th century, divided into [[see:natural astrology]] and [[see:judicial astrology]]; long confused with [[see:astronomy]], the two swapping places many times.
The branch of [[see:astrology]] foretelling tides, seasons and eclipses.
The branch of [[see:astrology]] foretelling how the stars affect human affairs.
Confused with [[see:naturalism]], as [[see:astronomy]] is with [[see:astrology]], which can lead people to judge you very differently.
Confused with [[see:naturism]], mirroring the confusion of [[see:astronomy]] and [[see:astrology]].
Divination by means of the stars, once a more common word for what we now call [[see:astrology]].
Like [[see:lunacy]], [[see:loony]] and [[see:moonstruck]], describes mental conditions once attributed to changes in the moon and tides.
A mental condition attributed to the moon, unfortunately also associated with femininity and monthly cycles.
Describes a mental condition once attributed to changes in the moon, like [[see:lunatic]].
Describes a mental condition once attributed to changes in the moon, like [[see:lunatic]].
Etymologically basically the same word as [[same-root:moon]], from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning to measure.
Has exactly the same history as [[same-root:month]]; its root, meaning to measure, also underlies [[same-root:meter]] and [[same-root:geometry]].
Linked to [[same-root:moon]] and [[same-root:month]] through [[same-root:menses]].
Basically means monthlies, overlapping with [[same-root:month]] and [[same-root:moon]].
Shares the root meaning to measure with [[same-root:moon]] and [[same-root:month]].
Shares the root meaning to measure with [[same-root:moon]] and [[same-root:month]].
Shares the root meaning to measure with [[same-root:moon]] and [[same-root:month]].
Shares the root meaning to measure with [[same-root:moon]] and [[same-root:month]].
Shares the root meaning to measure with [[same-root:moon]] and [[same-root:month]].
Shares the root meaning to measure with [[same-root:moon]] and [[same-root:month]].
Shares the root meaning to measure with [[same-root:moon]] and [[same-root:month]].
Now odd or whimsical; originally astronomical, meaning out of the center, for planets thought not to orbit with Earth at the center of their path.
A modern example, like [[see:eccentric]], of describing human quirks in terms of space.
A measurement term for the Moon's farthest point, now used for a climax or high point of any kind.
Used in astronomy and navigation by the stars for the line perpendicular to the horizon.
Originally the position of a planet in the zodiac where it exerts the greatest influence; the hosts recall [[see:exaltation of larks]].
A collective noun from an earlier episode, recalled alongside [[see:exaltation]].
Common in 14th-century astronomy and astrology for the effect of two planets on one another.
Given a silent letter by classicists keen to show its origin in Latin [[from:recepta]]; mentioned alongside [[see:reception]].
Popularised through astronomical language, implying coincidences were caused by the stars.
Meaning to be identical in substance or nature, popularised through astronomy along with [[see:coincidence]].
Popularised by astronomy, where it means a heavenly body being on the meridian.
The planet is named for its apparent speed, like the god Mercury, counterpart of [[see:Hermes]]; the metal, also [[see:quicksilver]], is named for its movement.
A name for the metal [[see:Mercury]]: silver that seems alive and moves quickly, with [[see:quick]] meaning lively.
In [[see:quicksilver]] it means lively or alive, as in [[see:quicklime]], [[see:quicksand]] and [[see:the quick and the dead]].
Uses [[see:quick]] in the same sense as [[see:quicksilver]].
An even better example of [[see:quick]] meaning alive, as in [[see:quicksilver]].
A theological phrase meaning the living and the dead, showing the old sense of [[see:quick]].
Named after the goddess of beauty and love, like [[see:Aphrodite]]; related to [[same-root:venery]]; in Old English called the [[see:morgensteorra]] or [[see:Lucifer]].
Related to [[same-root:Venus]], as touched on in the collective nouns episode.
Old English name for [[see:Venus]], which many now associate with [[see:Lucifer]].
Literally light-bringing; Old English name for [[see:Venus]] in the morning sky, an epithet of [[see:Diana]], and a name of [[see:Satan]] from Isaiah.
The name in the Greek text of Isaiah where English has [[see:Lucifer]]; also a god of Venus as morning star, brother of [[see:Hesperus]].
The evening star, brother of [[see:Phosphoros]].
Named after the war god, linked with [[see:Ares]], for its red colour visible from Earth; the Greeks called it [[see:Pyroeis]].
Greek name for [[see:Mars]], meaning the fiery.
A YA dystopian novel set on [[see:Mars]] that Jess is reading and recommends.
The largest planet, named for its size after the counterpart of [[see:Zeus]]; Jess says the Latin name means godfather.
Corresponds to [[see:Kronos]], a Titan son of [[see:Uranus]] and [[see:Gaia]]; associated with agriculture and bounty, celebrated in December at [[see:Saturnalia]].
The December festival of [[see:Saturn]], which dovetailed with [[see:Yuletide]] and contributed to Christmas being celebrated in December.
Corresponds to [[see:Hades]] and has been confused with [[see:Plutus]], a god of wealth; Jess insists it is still a planet.
[[see:Pluto]]'s status, which Jess notes still contains the word planet.

entries.term: my very early morning jam sandwich usually nourishes people
entries.note: Rob's planet mnemonic, still usable without the word for [[see:Pluto]]; Jess finds the jam sandwich very Paddington.

entries.term: my very easy method just speeds up naming planets
entries.note: A planet mnemonic that needs [[see:Pluto]] to work.

entries.term: my very educated mother just served us nine pizzas
entries.note: Jess's planet mnemonic, the pizzas standing for [[see:Pluto]]; Rob calls nine pizzas opulent.
A god of wealth confused with the Hades-like god behind [[see:Pluto]], the ending making all the difference.
About as old as English words get, always meaning the burning ball in the sky.
Something that protects you from the sun, containing [[from:sol]]; also used in French, and parallel to [[see:umbrella]] and [[see:parapluie]].
Means something that shades you from the sun, oddly parallel to [[see:parasol]].
French for umbrella, protecting you from the rain as a [[see:parasol]] protects you from the sun.
Named after [[from:Helios]], Greek for the sun, because it was detected in the solar spectrum during an eclipse in 1868.
